simulationInput.title: Simulation input
simulationInput.summary: Choose the disease, gene, variant, optional pathway, and run settings that drive the full simulation.
details: Changing any input should update every downstream panel.
The disease field sets the biological context, the gene and variant define the molecular trigger, and the pathway field narrows pathway context when needed.
Use external databases when you want live evidence-backed results; disable them if you want the local fallback model.

diseaseDiscovery.title: Disease discovery
diseaseDiscovery.summary: Ranks disease-linked genes and explains why the leading candidate is selected.
details: This panel maps the selected disease to likely genes using external evidence when available.
Each gene card shows the gene's function, its disease link, and why it ranks highly.

mutationEngine.title: Mutation engine
mutationEngine.summary: Interprets the variant text and turns it into a mutation type the simulator can use.
details: HGVS-like text, RS IDs, and typed variants are normalized here.
If the gene and variant are incompatible, the app should surface that as an invalid combination instead of failing.

proteinEffect.title: Protein effect
proteinEffect.summary: Estimates how the variant changes protein activity, stability, and binding.
details: This is where structural and functional impact are approximated, including AlphaFold-style structural context.
The card summarizes the remaining activity and the likely loss of function.

pathwaySimulator.title: Pathway simulator
pathwaySimulator.summary: Propagates the gene effect through a pathway graph and marks the processes that shift.
details: This panel shows how a single gene change can move through connected biological pathways.
Each bubble explains what the node does, how it changes, and how it affects the rest of the pathway.

cellPhenotype.title: Cell phenotype
cellPhenotype.summary: Converts pathway disruption into cell-level behavior such as proliferation, repair, and apoptosis.
details: This panel shows what the altered cell is likely doing: dividing more, repairing less, or resisting death.
The visual anatomy is meant to make the state changes readable at a glance.

populationDynamics.title: Population dynamics
populationDynamics.summary: Projects whether the altered cell state stays rare or expands across a population.
details: This panel turns the one-cell story into a clone-growth story over time.
Use it to see whether the mutated fraction remains small or starts to expand.

ecosystemBehavior.title: Ecosystem behavior
ecosystemBehavior.summary: Places the simulated disease into a larger tissue or body-site context and highlights the affected organs or regions.
details: This panel should reflect the actual body parts or tissues involved in the selected disease, not an abstract middle layer.
It can show a single site or a multi-site pattern when the disease implies several linked tissues.

researchSummary.title: Research summary
researchSummary.summary: Compresses the full simulation into a short readout with the key disease, gene, variant, and risk values.
details: This panel is the final human-readable summary for the run.
It should be quick to scan and consistent with the detailed panels above.

disease.summary: Search for the disease, syndrome, or cancer context you want the simulator to model.
details: This is the clinical or biological context that anchors the rest of the simulation.
Changing the disease should change the candidate genes, pathway context, cell phenotype, and tissue-level model.

gene.summary: Search for the gene symbol that drives the simulation.
details: The selected gene is the molecular starting point for the protein, pathway, cell, population, and ecosystem layers.
If the disease and gene do not fit together, the simulator should treat the combination as invalid.

mutation.summary: Enter the mutation or variant notation to map onto the gene.
details: The app interprets the typed variant, figures out the variant class, and then applies that interpretation to the model.
Missense changes one amino acid, nonsense introduces a stop codon, frameshift shifts the reading frame, and synonymous leaves the amino acid unchanged.

pathway.summary: Optionally filter the pathway search to a specific Reactome pathway for the selected gene.
details: This field narrows the pathway context without changing the disease or gene selection.
Leave it empty if you want the simulator to infer the most relevant pathway from the evidence.

steps.summary: Set how many time steps the downstream simulations should run.
details: More steps give the population and ecosystem layers more room to diverge over time.
Fewer steps keep the run faster and the trajectory shorter.

useExternalDatabases.summary: Toggle live evidence sources on or off.
details: On means the app should prefer live Open Targets, ClinVar, Reactome, and UniProt evidence.
Off means the simulator should use the local curated fallback model.
examples: On for live Open Targets, ClinVar, Reactome, and UniProt evidence
Off for the local fallback model

variant.summary: A variant is a change in the DNA or RNA sequence linked to the selected gene. The current class can be missense, nonsense, frameshift, deletion, insertion, duplication, or splice-site change.
details: The class matters because it changes how strongly the simulator expects the protein to be altered.
If the selected gene and variant do not match the same biological object, the app should say invalid combination.

aminoAcidChange.summary: Amino acid change means the specific residue-level substitution implied by the variant. It shows exactly which residue changed, such as R→H at position 175.
details: This tells the user which amino acid was present first and what it became after the mutation.
If the notation does not change the amino acid directly, explain that the protein-level effect is inferred from the coding change.

clinvarClassification.summary: ClinVar classification summarizes how the variant has been interpreted in clinical databases. Explain the range of possible classifications and what the current one means.
details: Common labels include pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign, benign, and unknown.
Pathogenic and likely pathogenic suggest stronger disease relevance, while uncertain significance means the evidence is still incomplete.

protein.summary: Protein is the translated molecule produced by the gene. It is the molecule doing the work that the gene encodes, and the simulation shows how the mutation changes that work.
details: This is the molecular machine or regulator whose activity is being changed by the mutation.
Use the current protein summary to explain the real biological role of the selected protein.

domainHit.summary: A domain hit means the variant lands in a functional region of the protein rather than a random part of the sequence. Explain what that domain does and why it matters.
details: Domains are compact functional regions such as DNA-binding regions, kinase domains, catalytic domains, or interaction motifs.
A hit in a key domain can have a larger effect than a change in a less constrained region.

selectedReactomePathway.summary: Selected Reactome pathway is the pathway specifically chosen for the run. If one is not selected, the simulator may infer the most relevant pathway from the gene and disease context.
details: This label tells the user which Reactome pathway is being used to drive the pathway graph.
It helps distinguish live pathway evidence from the simulator-generated fallback pathway.

candidateGene.summary: A ranked gene is one that is linked to the selected disease and shows a strong biological fit for the run.
details: The card should show the gene summary, the ranking score, and the evidence reason in plain language.
Hovering the candidate should give a short readable definition, not only a numeric score.

pathwayNode.summary: A pathway node is one step in the pathway graph. It can be the gene, a downstream process, a pathway bridge, or a disease-context node.
details: Gene/protein nodes represent the direct molecular target.
Process nodes represent downstream steps that summarize biological activity in the model.

remainingActivity.summary: Remaining activity shows how much of the protein's modelled function is left after the mutation. The value is a normalized model score from 0.00 to 1.00, not a literal laboratory percentage.
details: 0.30 means the model is treating the protein as having about 30% of its baseline activity remaining.
1.00 means no modeled loss; 0.00 means the model predicts full loss in this simplified scale.

remainingStability.summary: Remaining stability shows how structurally stable the protein is after the mutation. It is a 0.00 to 1.00 normalized score, not a raw assay percent.
details: A lower score means the model expects the protein to be less stable or easier to misfold.
0.30 means about 30% of the model's stability capacity remains.

remainingBinding.summary: Remaining binding shows how much binding capacity is left for partners, DNA, or cofactors. The score runs from 0.00 to 1.00 as a normalized model output.
details: Lower values mean the variant is likely to weaken interaction with key partners.
0.30 means about 30% of the modeled binding capacity remains.

lossOfFunctionScore.summary: Loss-of-function score estimates how strongly the mutation damages the protein's normal role. It is a normalized 0.00 to 1.00 score, where higher means more loss.
details: This is the inverse of remaining function: higher loss-of-function means a stronger impact.
0.70 means the simulator thinks the protein has lost much of its normal behavior, while 0.20 means only a modest effect.

proliferation.summary: Proliferation is the model's estimate of how strongly the cell keeps dividing. It is a normalized 0.00 to 1.00 score, where higher means more division pressure.
details: 0.30 means the cell is modeling low proliferative drive compared with baseline.
1.00 means the model is pushing the cell toward maximal growth pressure in the current scale.

apoptosis.summary: Apoptosis is the model's estimate of programmed cell death activity. It is normalized from 0.00 to 1.00, where higher means more cell death tendency.
details: 0.30 means the model expects apoptosis to be partially reduced or partially active depending on context.
1.00 means the model is strongly favoring cell death signaling.

repairCapacity.summary: Repair capacity measures how well the cell can fix damage in the current model. It is a normalized score from 0.00 to 1.00.
details: 0.30 means the model thinks repair ability is substantially reduced compared with baseline.
1.00 means repair capacity is effectively intact in the simplified simulator.

genomicInstability.summary: Genomic instability measures how error-prone the cell is becoming. It is a normalized 0.00 to 1.00 score, where higher means greater instability.
details: 0.30 means the model is showing some instability but not a full collapse of genomic control.
1.00 means the simulation is treating the genome as highly unstable in this simplified scale.

finalMutatedFraction.summary: Final mutated fraction is the share of the simulated population that is mutated at the end of the run. It is a normalized fraction from 0.00 to 1.00, not a percent you must manually convert.
details: 0.30 means roughly 30% of the simulated cells are mutated by the end of the run.
1.00 means the entire modeled population has become mutated in this simplified projection.

clonalExpansionScore.summary: Clonal expansion score measures how strongly the mutated clone is expanding across the population. It is a 0.00 to 1.00 normalized model score.
details: 0.30 means the clone is growing, but not aggressively, in the simulator.
1.00 means the model is strongly favoring rapid clonal expansion.

tumorLikeBurden.summary: Tumor-like burden estimates how much disease-like mass or burden is present in the tissue context. It is a normalized 0.00 to 1.00 score.
details: 0.30 means the tissue is showing a moderate amount of tumor-like burden in the model.
1.00 means the simulator is treating the burden as very high in the current scale.

immuneClearance.summary: Immune clearance estimates how well the immune system is removing the disease burden. It is normalized from 0.00 to 1.00, where higher means better clearance.
details: 0.30 means immune removal is weak or only partially effective in the current model.
1.00 means immune clearance is modeled as very strong.

inflammation.summary: Inflammation measures how much inflammatory pressure the tissue is under. It is a normalized 0.00 to 1.00 score.
details: 0.30 means the model is showing modest inflammation.
1.00 means inflammation is maximized in the simplified ecosystem scale.

ecosystemRisk.summary: Ecosystem risk combines the tissue, immune, and disease context into a single risk estimate. It is normalized from 0.00 to 1.00.
details: 0.30 means the model considers the broader tissue environment to be at a moderate risk level.
1.00 means the ecosystem layer is modeling very high overall risk.

missense.summary: Missense variants change one amino acid for another. The simulator should call this out whenever the notation changes a single residue in the protein.
details: Missense variants often affect function without removing the whole protein.
The current mutation should be described as the exact residue change when possible.

nonsense.summary: Nonsense variants create a premature stop codon and usually shorten the protein.
details: This often removes important domains from the protein.
This usually means the protein is truncated early.

frameshift.summary: Frameshift variants change the reading frame and alter many amino acids downstream.
details: These variants often produce a very different or truncated protein sequence.
They can have a larger impact than a single-residue substitution.

splice.summary: Splice-site variants alter how RNA is cut and stitched together before translation.
details: This can remove exons, keep introns, or shift the protein product.
The effect depends on where the splice change occurs.

synonymous.summary: Synonymous variants change the DNA code without changing the amino acid sequence.
details: They can still matter if they affect splicing, expression, or RNA stability.
In many cases the protein sequence stays unchanged.

inframe.summary: In-frame variants add or remove amino acids without shifting the reading frame.
details: The protein remains in frame, but a short segment is altered.
The effect depends on whether the changed segment is functionally important.

deletion.summary: Deletion variants remove DNA or amino-acid sequence from the gene product.
details: The severity depends on whether the deletion shifts the reading frame.
Small deletions may be in-frame; larger ones may be frameshift deletions.

insertion.summary: Insertion variants add extra DNA or amino-acid sequence into the gene product.
details: The effect depends on whether the insertion preserves the reading frame.
Insertions in important domains can be disruptive even when short.

duplication.summary: Duplication variants repeat a stretch of DNA or amino-acid sequence.
details: Duplications can preserve the reading frame or shift it depending on length.
The functional effect depends on where the duplication occurs.

unknown.summary: Unknown variant class means the notation could not be cleanly mapped into a known HGVS-style category.
details: The simulator should still explain what it can infer from the text.
If the gene and mutation are incompatible, the app should flag that instead of crashing.
